days.title: Diagnostic & project hygiene
days.tagline: Measure the gaps. Then fix only the ones that matter.
days.outcome: A scored baseline diagnostic, a clean local Python project, and a tested first commit.

tier.name: Local laptop + GitHub + Databricks Free Edition
tier.status: Free for this lab. Databricks signup only today; no compute is needed. Public GitHub repos are available on the free plan. Check account-specific eligibility.

concepts.title: From notebook to product
concepts.body: Exploratory notebooks are excellent for research. A delivered AI application additionally needs repeatable installs, tests, configuration, safe inputs, and predictable failures.

concepts.title: Your two-hour diagnostic
concepts.body: Set a two-hour timer during BUILD. Work independently: Python (30 min), SQL (30 min), Pandas (30 min), ML reasoning (30 min). Write down where you were slow. Do not ask AI for the answer before attempting.

concepts.title: Quality gate
concepts.body: Typing, linting, tests and environment variables are not ceremony. They let a colleague change your code without guessing what it does, and keep secrets out of Git.

tasks.title: Python diagnostic • 30 min
tasks.brief: Given a list of strings, nulls, and corrupt entries, implement a function returning the sum of valid non-negative integers and the number of invalid values. Decide whether negatives are invalid; document your choice.
tasks.deliverable: A Python function plus 4 edge-case tests.
hints: Make parsing and validation separate decisions. Ask what each invalid case should do.
Try iterating once, calling int() only inside try/except, and counting invalid items.
Pseudocode: initialize total and invalid; for each item: try parse; if not parseable or negative count invalid; else add; return pair.

tasks.title: SQL diagnostic • 30 min
tasks.brief: Use SQLite or your SQL editor. Create a tiny orders table and answer: revenue by customer, customers with zero orders, and the most recent order per customer. You may use JOINs or a window function.
tasks.deliverable: Save the SQL file and the output of each query.
hints: There are separate questions about aggregation, missing matches, and latest rows.
GROUP BY handles revenue; LEFT JOIN exposes missing matches; ROW_NUMBER can rank orders.
Pseudocode: group orders by customer for revenue; left join customers to orders for zero orders; rank per customer by date then order id.
checks: Include a customer with zero orders

tasks.title: Pandas diagnostic • 30 min
tasks.brief: Create a 10-row table with missing values and duplicates. Clean it without a row-wise Python loop. Compute a grouped summary. Explain what you did with missing data.
tasks.deliverable: A short notebook or Python file with before/after row counts.
hints: Pandas columns are whole arrays, not just lists of records.
Look at drop_duplicates, fillna, groupby, and how filtering treats missing values.
Pseudocode: inspect null counts; remove duplicates by business key; handle missing columns with a stated rule; aggregate by category.

tasks.title: ML reasoning diagnostic • 30 min
tasks.brief: Explain in your own words: leakage, a suitable classification baseline, precision vs recall for missed payment prediction, and why an accuracy-only report can deceive.
tasks.deliverable: Four short answers, each with a failure example.
hints: Think about what is known at prediction time.
A feature collected after the label outcome may leak the answer.
Pseudocode: define timestamp of prediction; list known features; remove future-only features; choose baseline; evaluate beyond one metric.

tasks.title: Build the project skeleton • 90 min
tasks.brief: Create .venv, pyproject.toml, src/, tests/, .gitignore and README. Install pytest and ruff. Implement one function from the diagnostic with a test. Run pytest and ruff locally. Use venv + pip today; uv is optional, not required.
tasks.deliverable: A tested, linted repository with no secrets, datasets, or virtual environment checked in.
hints: Keep production code separate from tests, and never store tokens in Git.
Use python -m venv .venv, pip install pytest ruff, and run python -m pytest followed by ruff check .
Pseudocode: create folders; make environment; add dependencies; write function; write test; run checks; commit only source/config/documentation.

break.title: Deliberately commit a secret — safely simulate, never use a real key
break.challenge: Create a dummy string called EXAMPLE_TOKEN and verify whether .gitignore excludes .env but NOT committed Python source. Remove the dummy string and write a rule: secrets belong in environment variables and a secret manager, never in source.
break.diagnose: git status and git diff --cached reveal exactly what would be committed; .gitignore does not erase tracked files.

quiz.question: Which file normally should NOT go to a public repository?
quiz.explanation: .env commonly contains secrets. Commit an .env.example with placeholder names instead.

quiz.question: What does pytest primarily provide?
quiz.explanation: pytest runs repeatable tests; it does not train models.

quiz.question: A feature measured after the target event is often…
quiz.explanation: Post-outcome features can make test metrics falsely optimistic.

quiz.question: Why use a virtual environment?
quiz.explanation: Separate environments help reproduce installs and avoid conflicts.

quiz.question: What does ruff check do?
quiz.explanation: Ruff is a fast Python linter and formatter; linting is not a substitute for tests.

cheatsheet: Pure function = same input, same result, no outside side effects.
Use type hints for contracts; validate untrusted inputs at runtime.
Never commit .env, credentials, private data, or large model weights.
Leakage: data from the future or data derived from the label.
pytest validates behavior; ruff catches many static quality issues.
A reproducible README has install, run, test, assumptions and limitations.
interview: Tell me about your last ML project. How would you make it reproducible for another engineer?
How do you catch leakage before training rather than after a suspiciously high score?
What do you unit-test in an ML data-cleaning function, and what requires integration tests?
ship: Git commit: day01: diagnostic and project scaffold
README: show commands, test result and actual gaps
Draft bullet: Built a reproducible Python project with X passing tests and lint checks (replace X after running).

days.title: SQL + Python essentials
days.outcome: Correct JOIN, CTE and window queries, vectorized Pandas transformation, and unit-tested Python exceptions.

tier.name: SQLite + Python + Pandas, local
tier.status: Free. No cloud or GPU. SQLite ships with Python; Pandas is open-source. Install using your own virtual environment.

concepts.title: SQL grain is everything
concepts.body: Before joining tables, state what one row represents. An accidental one-to-many JOIN can duplicate amounts and silently corrupt revenue totals.

concepts.title: CTE versus window function
concepts.body: CTEs name intermediate queries. A window function computes values across a partition while retaining individual rows. A GROUP BY collapses rows.

concepts.title: Vectorization and boundaries
concepts.body: In Pandas, operate on columns where possible; validate input schemas and explicitly handle errors at system boundaries.

tasks.title: SQL: rank overdue invoices • 80 min
tasks.brief: Create customers and invoices. Find latest invoice per customer using ROW_NUMBER; calculate overdue total only for unpaid invoices; include customers with no invoices. Include duplicates and tied timestamps in your tests.
tasks.deliverable: queries.sql, expected outputs, and explanation of join cardinality.
hints: Start by describing the grain of each table and the output.
Use a CTE for ranked invoices; PARTITION BY customer_id, ORDER BY invoice_date DESC, invoice_id DESC.
Pseudocode: join customer to ranked invoice rows; filter to rank=1 for latest; separately sum unpaid overdue amounts; left join aggregates.

reference.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE invoices(customer TEXT, invoice_id INT, amount INT);
INSERT INTO invoices VALUES ('A', 1, 50), ('A', 2, 70), ('B', 3, 20);
""")
rows = con.execute("""
WITH ranked AS (
 SELECT customer, invoice_id, amount,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY invoice_id DESC) AS rn
 FROM invoices
) SELECT customer, amount FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY customer
""").fetchall()
print(rows)

tasks.title: Pandas: cleaning without apply • 65 min
tasks.brief: Create a deliberately messy CSV with invoice_id, customer_id, amount, invoice_date and paid. Reject negative amounts; calculate totals by customer using column operations. Compare your cleaned count to your own expected count.
tasks.deliverable: clean.py plus a tiny fixture and 3 tests.
hints: Prefer an explicit cleaning policy over silent dropna calls.
Try pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce"), boolean masks, and groupby.
Pseudocode: coerce amount to number; count failed parses; filter amount >= 0; groupby customer and sum; assert totals.
checks: No Python for-loop across DataFrame rows

tasks.title: Python: dataclasses and errors • 65 min
tasks.brief: Create an Invoice dataclass and a function that parses a dictionary, raises a helpful ValueError for malformed amount, and never hides all exceptions with except Exception: pass. Test good and bad cases.
tasks.deliverable: invoice.py, tests and a short decision note.
hints: Use a dataclass for a small, typed record.
Explicitly distinguish missing fields from invalid formats.
Pseudocode: read fields; validate required keys; convert amount; reject negative; construct immutable record; raise targeted exceptions.

break.title: The duplicated JOIN
break.challenge: Insert two invoices for the same customer. Join invoices to customer-level totals and sum both totals again. Observe the overcount. Repair the grain or aggregate before joining.
break.diagnose: Write the number of rows before/after the JOIN, then explain the mismatch.

quiz.question: ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY does what?
quiz.explanation: Window functions retain rows and add group-relative calculations.

quiz.question: LEFT JOIN keeps which unmatched rows?
quiz.explanation: LEFT JOIN retains every left-side row.

quiz.question: Why might SUM be doubled after a JOIN?
quiz.explanation: One-to-many joins can multiply measures.

quiz.question: Which tends to be better than iterrows for a column calculation?
quiz.explanation: Vectorization is usually simpler and often faster.

quiz.question: A bare except followed by pass is risky because…
quiz.explanation: Hidden failures can corrupt outputs and mask production incidents.

cheatsheet: Define grain before any JOIN.
GROUP BY collapses; window functions annotate.
ROW_NUMBER requires deterministic ORDER BY for stable results.
CTEs improve organization, not necessarily performance.
Vectorize Pandas operations and validate null policy.
Catch specific exceptions; do not hide failures.
interview: How would you debug a revenue total that doubled after a JOIN?
Explain when you would use ROW_NUMBER versus GROUP BY.
How do you handle malformed records in a production data pipeline?
ship: Commit SQL and Python drills with fixtures and tests.
Record the actual query outputs and failures fixed.
Draft bullet: Created tested SQL/Pandas transformations with X quality assertions (only once measured).

days.title: FastAPI + Docker
days.tagline: Your first tiny service with an honest contract.
days.outcome: A working prediction-like API stub with request validation, health endpoint, tests, and a local container.

tier.name: FastAPI, Pydantic, Docker or Podman
tier.status: Free when running locally. Docker Desktop licensing depends on organization size/use; use free Podman if not eligible. Verify currently installed package versions before the lab; avoid unpinned production versions.

concepts.title: HTTP contracts
concepts.body: A request has method, path, headers and body. Your API should validate untrusted input, return understandable errors, and respond predictably.

concepts.title: Pydantic + FastAPI
concepts.body: Pydantic validates typed request models at runtime. FastAPI uses these types to generate OpenAPI documentation. Validation is not authentication.

concepts.title: Container boundaries
concepts.body: Docker packages your application and dependencies. It does not automatically secure your API or guarantee observability.

tasks.title: Create /health and /score endpoints • 90 min
tasks.brief: Make /health return a stable status. Define a strict request schema for an invoice with amount and days_overdue. Implement your OWN scoring rule as a temporary deterministic stub, labeled a rule, not an ML model.
tasks.deliverable: main.py, sample request/response, and API contract in README.
hints: Start with a pure function separate from the web endpoint.
Use a Pydantic BaseModel with Field constraints; then call your function from a POST route.
Pseudocode: parse request model; reject negative amount; compute a simple rule; serialize score and rule version.

reference.expected: After `uvicorn main:app --reload`, GET /health returns {"status":"ok"}; POST /score with {"amount":200,"days_overdue":45} returns {"risk_flag":true,"kind":"rule_only"}.
reference.run: pip install fastapi uvicorn && uvicorn main:app --reload

checks: Do not call stub an ML model

tasks.title: Write endpoint tests • 60 min
tasks.brief: Test GET /health, valid POST, and invalid POST with negative amount. Verify the error is a 4xx, not a 500.
hints: HTTP testing checks both status codes and response bodies.
Use fastapi.testclient.TestClient; httpx is required by TestClient and must be installed.
Pseudocode: create client; call routes; assert expected status and response; send invalid input and assert validation error.

tasks.title: Containerize and smoke-test • 60 min
tasks.brief: Create a small Python Dockerfile, install pinned requirements after checking versions, expose port 8000, and test the app from your laptop. Do not copy .env into the image.
hints: A container needs a working directory, dependencies, source and a foreground process.
Use python:3.12-slim, WORKDIR, COPY requirements, pip install, COPY app, and CMD uvicorn.
Pseudocode: build image; run with port mapping; GET /health; inspect logs; stop container.

break.title: Invalid request path
break.challenge: Send {"amount":-10,"days_overdue":45} to /score. Observe the validation response. Then send a string where a number is expected and explain coercion/strict-mode tradeoffs.
break.diagnose: Distinguish 422 validation errors from 500 programming errors; capture the real HTTP status.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method is most natural for scoring a JSON body?
quiz.explanation: POST accepts a request body with explicit input data.

quiz.question: Does Pydantic replace authorization?
quiz.explanation: Input validation and access control address different risks.

quiz.question: An invalid input should usually result in…
quiz.explanation: Return a meaningful 4xx code when the client sends invalid data.

quiz.question: Does a Dockerfile keep secrets out automatically?
quiz.explanation: Avoid copying .env and supply secrets at runtime.

quiz.question: What is a health check for?
quiz.explanation: Health endpoints indicate if a service is alive; they do not prove predictions are correct.

cheatsheet: GET reads; POST submits data.
422 often indicates FastAPI/Pydantic validation errors.
Request schema is a contract; reject unsafe inputs.
Business logic belongs outside route handlers.
Container ≠ secure deployment; manage secrets and dependencies.
Test valid, invalid, and boundary requests.
interview: What would you change before exposing this API to a customer?
Why test the pure scoring function separately from the FastAPI endpoint?
How do you avoid leaking credentials in a Docker image?
ship: Commit FastAPI app, tests and Dockerfile.
Record actual curl samples and container run result.
Draft bullet: Built a containerized FastAPI service with X tested endpoints (replace X after your run).

days.title: Databricks & Spark
days.tagline: Think in distributed dataframes, even with tiny data.
days.outcome: A working PySpark data transformation, an explained execution plan, and an agreed Project 1 business problem.

tier.name: Databricks Free Edition serverless compute
tier.status: Free Edition has fair-use quotas, only serverless compute, and no reliability SLA. Workspace quotas vary; do not assume unlimited hours. Local PySpark is a free fallback. No GPU is needed.

concepts.title: Why Spark exists
concepts.body: Spark distributes operations over partitions. Your code describes a transformation graph; Spark can wait until an action like count() triggers work.

concepts.title: Transformations vs actions
concepts.body: select, filter, join and groupBy describe changes. count, collect and show cause computation. Avoid collect on large datasets.

concepts.title: Free Edition reality
concepts.body: Use a small dataset. Spark is valuable for learning scalable patterns, but Pandas is often simpler and cheaper for data that fits memory.

tasks.title: Run your first Spark DataFrame • 65 min
tasks.brief: In Databricks, create an in-memory toy payments table and compute total amount by customer. Inspect the result and explain what triggered execution.
tasks.deliverable: Notebook with actual outputs and your explanation of lazy execution.
hints: Create a DataFrame with customer_id and amount using spark.createDataFrame.
Try groupBy(...).sum(...), then orderBy(...), then show().
Pseudocode: create rows; transform with groupBy; aggregate sum; run action; verify hand-calculated totals.

reference.code:
# Run in a Databricks Python notebook where `spark` exists.
rows = [("A", 50), ("A", 70), ("B", 20)]
df = spark.createDataFrame(rows, ["customer", "amount"])
result = df.groupBy("customer").sum("amount").orderBy("customer")
print([(r["customer"], r["sum(amount)"]) for r in result.collect()])
reference.run: Databricks Python notebook with an active Free Edition serverless session

checks: No collect on a large real dataset

tasks.title: Join and inspect a query plan • 75 min
tasks.brief: Create a separate customer table (including a customer with no payments), LEFT JOIN to the payments, and compare physical/optimized plans with a simple join. Watch for duplicate rows.
tasks.deliverable: Screenshot or text of explain() and a short join-grain note.
hints: Think: What is one row of each table?
Use DataFrame.join(..., "left") and explain() to inspect the plan.
Pseudocode: create customer table; left join; count rows and customer ids; compare plan; explain potential shuffle.

tasks.title: Scope Project 1 • 70 min
tasks.brief: Choose an openly licensed business dataset suitable for predicting payment delays or late-payment likelihood. Inspect its actual licence, timestamp fields, label, and leakage risks. If licence or data is unclear, create a labeled synthetic sample ONLY for pipeline development and defer model claims.
tasks.deliverable: A problem.md with user, decision, label, prediction time, metric and leakage checklist.
hints: A business problem needs a user and a decision, not just a Kaggle CSV.
Prefer a target available after prediction time and features available before it. Verify licence at source.
Pseudocode: define business action → prediction event → allowed features → baseline → holdout → acceptance metric.
checks: Success metric grounded in business costs

break.title: The accidental collect()
break.challenge: Explain why df.collect() on millions of rows can crash a small driver. Rework your notebook to use show(10), limit, or aggregate first. Do not intentionally overload the free compute quota.
break.diagnose: Record where work happens: Spark executors vs Python driver.

quiz.question: Spark select and filter are generally…
quiz.explanation: Transformations build a plan; actions start execution.

quiz.question: Which can pull an entire dataset to the driver?
quiz.explanation: collect() transfers all returned rows to the driver.

quiz.question: Why inspect JOIN cardinality?
quiz.explanation: Wrong join grain can silently duplicate data.

quiz.question: When would you NOT use Spark?
choices: Small in-memory dataset with simple operations
quiz.explanation: Pandas/SQL may be simpler for modest workloads.

quiz.question: A dataset without a verified licence should be…
quiz.explanation: Validate reuse and redistribution rights before publishing data.

cheatsheet: DataFrames are lazy transformation plans.
Actions include count/show/collect.
Avoid collecting large data to the driver.
Join grain must be explicitly checked.
Free Edition can have quota shutdowns.
Define a timestamp-aware prediction problem before modeling.
interview: Explain lazy execution in Spark to a junior engineer.
How do you choose between Pandas, SQL and Spark for a customer pipeline?
What questions would you ask a customer before building payment-delay prediction?
ship: Commit Spark notebook or scripts, not credentials.
Add the real explain() output and dataset licence evidence.
Draft bullet: Built an initial PySpark transformation over X records with validated totals (measure X).

days.title: Delta, quality & medallion
days.tagline: Build data you can trust before building a model.
days.outcome: A small bronze/silver/gold pipeline with explicit data-quality tests and repeatable evidence.

tier.name: Databricks Free Edition + Delta tables
tier.status: Free Edition compute is quota-bound; availability of Unity Catalog permissions and specific workspace features must be checked in your account. Local Python/Parquet can teach the cleaning pattern if Delta features are unavailable.

concepts.title: Bronze, silver, gold are conventions
concepts.body: Bronze: preserve raw source with provenance. Silver: clean, type and de-duplicate. Gold: business-ready aggregates or model features. These are architecture labels, not built-in Spark classes.

concepts.title: Delta Lake and transactional data
concepts.body: Delta Lake adds a transaction log and table operations on top of files. Avoid promising every enterprise feature is enabled in Free Edition.

concepts.title: Data quality as code
concepts.body: Define checks for null keys, duplicate business IDs, valid ranges, and plausible dates. Decide whether to reject, quarantine or repair bad records; never silently discard without evidence.

tasks.title: Ingest a reproducible bronze table • 60 min
tasks.brief: Read a small CSV of invoices (or the vetted dataset from Day 4) into a named bronze table or DataFrame. Include source_file and ingestion_time. Show total row count and raw null counts. Do not overwrite your raw copy.
tasks.deliverable: Notebook output, row counts and provenance fields.
hints: Raw means recoverable, not cleaned in place.
Use explicit column names; include a reproducible source reference.
Pseudocode: read source; add ingestion metadata; write raw table; count rows; log source version.

tasks.title: Silver transforms with quality gates • 95 min
tasks.brief: Normalize types, deduplicate on invoice_id with a documented rule, reject negative amounts, and count bad records. Prove that repeated ingestion does not multiply rows.
tasks.deliverable: Silver table, quality_checks.py, observed pass/fail counts.
hints: Write quality rules before changing records.
Check null IDs and amounts, duplicate IDs, date ordering, and permitted values.
Pseudocode: load bronze; validate fields; split valid/quarantine; resolve duplicates by timestamp; assert unique keys; save silver.

reference.code:
rows = [
 {"invoice_id":"1", "amount":100},
 {"invoice_id":"1", "amount":100},
 {"invoice_id":"2", "amount":-8},
 {"invoice_id":"3", "amount":25},
]
seen, good, rejected = set(), [], 0
for row in rows:
    if row["amount"] < 0 or row["invoice_id"] in seen:
        rejected += 1
        continue
    seen.add(row["invoice_id"])
    good.append(row)
print(len(good), rejected)

checks: Repeated input does not multiply silver rows

tasks.title: Gold aggregate + repeatable run • 55 min
tasks.brief: Create a gold view with customer-level invoice count, total amount and max overdue days. Document that these are descriptive today: do not leak future labels into later model features. Re-run from raw and compare counts.
tasks.deliverable: Gold schema and a README table with actual quality metrics.
hints: Gold is tailored for consumers; it is not necessarily a machine-learning feature table yet.
Use groupBy/SQL GROUP BY with explicit allowed columns; save observed row counts.
Pseudocode: read silver → group by customer → compute business aggregates → assert row and sum invariants → store gold.

break.title: The quiet duplicate
break.challenge: Reingest the same source into your silver step. If your logic simply appends, duplicates appear. Debug and fix using stable business keys and idempotent writes for your chosen environment.
break.diagnose: Compare key uniqueness and counts across two identical runs; record before/after evidence.

quiz.question: What should bronze preserve?
quiz.explanation: Bronze stores source data so transformations can be reproduced.

quiz.question: What does idempotence mean here?
choices: Repeated identical runs yield the same state
quiz.explanation: Idempotent pipelines can be safely rerun.

quiz.question: A null primary business key should usually be…
choices: Explicitly rejected/quarantined or handled under a rule
quiz.explanation: Null identifiers can break deduplication and joins.

quiz.question: Does MLflow automatically calculate PSI drift?
quiz.explanation: You must implement or integrate drift checks; MLflow tracking alone does not detect drift.

quiz.question: Gold should be designed around…
quiz.explanation: Gold tables represent curated business needs or downstream features.

cheatsheet: Bronze raw; silver validated; gold consumer-ready.
Document source, licence, provenance and ingestion time.
Define data-quality checks before cleaning.
Quarantine or count bad records; do not hide them.
Idempotence avoids duplicate accumulation on reruns.
Quality metrics need observed counts, not invented percentages.
interview: Design a bronze/silver/gold pipeline for messy vendor invoices.
How do you deal with a source that republishes the same records every day?
What data-quality tests would prevent silent corruption before model training?
ship: Commit pipeline source, tests and a measured quality report.
README includes actual source licence and row-count table.
Draft bullet: Built a bronze/silver/gold pipeline with X automated quality checks and repeatable reruns (measure X).
